conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and this is a judgment-free space. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll move through one question at a own pace, and it usually takes only a few minutes.  

Ready to begin?  

First, thinking back over the past seven days: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

*sighs softly, eyes a bit downcast*

Honestly... it's been pretty hard to find anything funny lately. When my husband tries to make jokes like he used to, I just... I don't know, I can't seem to laugh. I try to smile for him, but it feels forced. Everything just feels so heavy right now, even when I know something should be amusing. It used to be so easy to laugh before the baby came, and now it's like that part of me is just... buried under all this exhaustion and worry.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little chuckle when my older niece made a silly face at the baby, but even that felt forced—like I was pretending more than actually feeling amused. Most of the time nothing feels funny; it just feels flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice quiet*

Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with friends, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower. Now when I think about doing any of those, it feels kind of pointless. I still try to plan them, hoping the feeling will come back, but it’s like the enjoyment part never shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes welling up*

Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn't stop crying for almost an hour, and I kept thinking it must be something I'm doing wrong. Maybe I'm not feeding him right, or I'm holding him wrong... even when my mom said sometimes babies just cry, I couldn't shake the feeling that it's my fault. The other night when he spit up so much after feeding, I just sat there crying, telling my husband I must be doing something terrible as a mother.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods, rubbing my hands together*

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep, everything’s quiet, and suddenly my heart starts racing. I’ll check if he’s breathing, then five minutes later I’m checking again. I worry the formula isn’t the right kind, that the room’s too cold, too hot, that I’ll drop him when I stand up—things that don’t even make sense. There’s this constant knot in my stomach like something awful is about to happen, even when nothing’s wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*swallows hard, voice shaky*

Yeah… it’s like the anxiety spikes even higher a few times a day. My chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something terrible is about to happen to the baby or to me. Last night I was rocking him and suddenly felt like the room was closing in—my heart was pounding so loud I thought it would wake him. I had to put him in the crib and go stand by the open window just to breathe. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, eyes filling again*

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in little tasks. I’ll start folding the laundry and hear the baby cry, then the dog needs out, the bottles need sterilizing, and I just freeze. Yesterday I sat on the floor amid piles of clothes and cried because I couldn’t figure out which thing to do first. Everyone keeps saying “sleep when the baby sleeps,” but during those short naps I’m running through everything I should be doing and feeling worse because I can’t keep up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*looks down, voice quiet*

Yeah… even when the baby finally settles, I lie there staring at the ceiling. My mind just keeps spinning—did I burp him long enough, is the monitor on, will he wake up in ten minutes? Last night I couldn’t fall asleep until after three, and then every tiny sound jolted me awake. I end up scrolling on my phone, hoping it’ll distract me, but the glow just makes it worse. I’m exhausted all day, yet when night comes my body won’t let me rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

*nods slowly, eyes damp*

Yes… most of the day, every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest. Even when I’m feeding him or changing him, there’s this constant sadness in the background. Yesterday I watched a video of him smiling and instead of feeling happy, I just started crying because I felt so empty. People keep saying I should be enjoying these early weeks, but mostly I just feel... gray.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*voice cracks, tears slipping down*

Yeah... it happens a few times a week now. Sometimes it's when the baby won't settle and I feel useless, but other times it just sneaks up—like this morning when I saw the sunrise through the window and suddenly I was sobbing. My husband found me crying over a nappy ad yesterday because it showed a happy mom singing to her baby, and I realized I can't remember the last time I sang to him without forcing myself. The tears just come and I can't stop them, even when I know I "should" be happy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, wiping eyes*

No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave my baby without a mom. I just want to feel better so I can take care of him the way he deserves.

I hear how heavy every day feels since your baby arrived-how laughter, joy, and even simple tasks now seem distant or pointless. You described a constant knot of worry, nightly battles with racing thoughts, and tears that arrive without warning, leaving you exhausted and convinced you're failing as a mom. Yet through this darkness you remain devoted to your son and determined to protect him, which speaks to your resilience even in the midst of such pain.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports virtually no spontaneous laughter, describing even rare chuckles as forced and emotionless, aligning with 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly reports frequent, intense self-blame ('I do that a lot,' 'couldn't shake the feeling that it's my fault') consistent with 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive, unprovoked anxiety with physical symptoms and repetitive intrusive worries, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple daily panic attacks with chest tightness, breathlessness, catastrophic thoughts, and needing to escape, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," using metaphors like "drowning" and reports being unable to prioritize or start tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia with racing anxious thoughts, inability to fall asleep until 3 a.m., repeated awakenings, and daytime exhaustion, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, emotional heaviness, inability to feel joy even with baby, and crying episodes — matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying episodes several times per week triggered by both stress and unexpected moments, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 exceeds the threshold of 13 indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The patient meets core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and insomnia nearly every day for the past three weeks. She also reports frequent panic symptoms, suggesting co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No self-harm ideation (<quote>I'd never want to leave my baby without a mom</quote>) is present. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Begin safety plan and monitor for emergence of self-harm thoughts
3. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>IPT</med> or <med>CBT</med> and consider antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding
4. Provide local 24/7 crisis line numbers and schedule follow-up within one week
5. Encourage 20-minute daytime rest periods and accept help with household tasks to reduce overwhelm
6. Offer printed resources on postpartum mood disorders and peer support group contacts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based interview, 0–3 weeks post-delivery.

Symptoms endorsed (all present ≥ daily):
- Marked anhedonia (loss of humor, anticipatory pleasure)
- Persistent low mood, “gray,” frequent crying spells
- Excessive self-blame / guilt over routine infant care
- Generalized & panic-level anxiety, no clear precipitant
- Somatic tension, chest tightness, hyper-arousal
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia unrelated to infant demands
- Overwhelm / “drowning,” executive freeze with daily tasks

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety; no psychotic or self-harm ideation reported.

Risk flags:
✓ Depressed mood + anhedonia + guilt  
✓ Anxiety interfering with infant care  
✓ Functional impairment (hygiene, household tasks)  
✗ No suicidal/homicidal thoughts; denies self-harm intent  

Screening conclusion: High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; recommend immediate formal evaluation (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and safety plan; consider expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist.
